items.note: Santosh Kumar Verma's outline of endowment mechanisms: akshayanivi provisions from the Satavahana period, land grants, growth under the Guptas, large post-Gupta temple land grants with special privileges.
items.gloss: Santosh Kumar Verma says that provisions of the akshayanivi system for managing religious institutions appear in the Satavahana period. Evidence of allotment of agricultural land also begins to appear widely, first mentioned in the inscriptions of Gautamiputra Satakarni and accounts of the Chutu rulers, who gave such donations to the viharas of Nagarjunakonda and Amaravati. In the Gupta period their number began to increase, where akshayanivi in the form of money and later nidhi, nyasa and nikshepa are mentioned by various smriti and other writers. The practice existed in the south too. After the Gupta period temples were given land grants on a large scale, with privileges like 'sandandashaparadha' and 'bhutopatapratyaya', which was to some extent a transfer of the exclusive rights of royal authority.

items.note: Precedents of royal land grants to monasteries: the Udayagiri inscriptions near Vidisha record Chandragupta II's commander giving such a grant to the Kakanadabota (Sanchi) mahavihara; Nalanda, Harsha and other institutions depended on such grants.
items.gloss: In the inscriptions of the famous Udayagiri near Vidisha we see Atrakakardava, commander of Chandragupta II Vikramaditya, making such a donation to the Kakanadabota (old name of Sanchi) mahavihara. In Kumaragupta's time royal patronage had a role in establishing a mahavihara and university like Nalanda, which Harsha extended by donating several hundred villages. Not only Nalanda, many other world-famous institutions of that era depended on land grants, from Vallabhi in the west to the Big Temple of the Chola kings in the south. These grants were called agrahara (to scholars or persons of religious importance), devadeya or mathapura.

items.note: Author's inference that Udaypur temple must have had a good budget with resources arranged by grants under Udayaditya; no inscription giving details has been found.
items.gloss: Looking at the vastness and grandeur of Udaypur, its budget must have been quite large from its economic and administrative side. Since Udayaditya was the ruler, resources for the temple must certainly have been arranged through such grants. No inscription giving detailed information on this has been found. If one is ever found, it may help in understanding the temple's economy.

items.note: Inscription on a pillar to the right of the temple's east door, cited in Indian Antiquary vols. 18 and 20, Gwalior Archaeological Dept report Samvat 1974 no. 121, Bhandarkar's list no. 483 and Kielhorn's list no. 207; 14 lines.
items.gloss: This inscription is on a pillar to the right of the temple's east door. It is cited in Indian Antiquary part 18 page 342 and part 20 page 83 no. 2 (1889); Annual Reports of the Archaeological Department Gwalior State Samvat 1974 no. 121; no. 483 in Bhandarkar's list of northern inscriptions and no. 207 in Kielhorn's list. This inscription is of 14 lines.
refs: Annual Reports of the Archaeological Department Gwalior State, Samvat 1974, no. 121
Bhandarkar, List of Northern Inscriptions, no. 483
Kielhorn, List of Inscriptions of Northern India, no. 207

items.note: Sanskrit, 13th-century Nagari lettering, rather crude letter forms, text unclear in places because of damage.
items.gloss: Its language is Sanskrit. It is in the fort and the letter forms are 13th-century Nagari. The letters are also quite crude in form. Because of decay the text is not clear in some places.

items.note: Dated VS 1286 (1229 CE), Kartik sudi, Friday (date end broken); records a gift of 4 biswa of land to the Udayeshvaradeva temple by treasury officer Dhamadeva in the reign of Maharaja Devapaladeva.
items.gloss: The date on this inscription is written Samvat 1286 (1229 CE) Kartik sudi ... Friday. The last part of the date is broken. The purpose of this inscription is to mention the donation of 4 biswa of land for the temple of Udayeshvaradeva by Dhamadeva, treasury officer, during the reign of Maharaja Devapaladeva.

items.note: Author argues that Devapaladeva, named only as Mahakumara here, probably held a military or administrative post at Udaypur before becoming king, so that Udaypur produced at least two Paramara kings.
items.gloss: It is worth noting that long before the date of the inscription Devapaladeva had sat on the throne in the capital Dhar and begun using full royal titles. Before becoming king he must have held some military or administrative responsibility at Udaypur, and hence in this inscription he is addressed only by the title Mahakumara. If he lived at Udaypur before becoming king, this fact raises Udaypur's importance, because about a hundred and fifty years earlier Udayaditya too must have been in such a role. Now it also becomes clear that Udaypur was a centre from which at least two princes of the Paramara dynasty emerged as kings.

items.note: The donated land is given as 4 biswa, now one-twentieth of a bigha, a very small plot; the measure was locally current in the Bhopal region.
items.gloss: In Devapaladeva's inscription the quantity of land donated is written as 4 biswa, which at present is a twentieth part of a bigha of land. A very small plot; this unit of land measurement was locally current in the Bhopal region.

items.note: Opening lines of the Devapaladeva inscription with Hindi translation: Samvat 1286 Kartik sudi (day lost), Friday, before the god Udayeshvara.
items.gloss: Let there be success. In the year Samvat 1286, Kartik sudi ____, on Friday, before the god Shri Udayeshvara ____.

items.note: Names Shri Devapaladeva's victorious reign and mentions a mahamudra office.
items.gloss: Shri Devapaladeva ... in the reign of the auspicious Shri Devapaladeva, associated with victory, in the business of the mahamudra ____.

items.note: The grant itself: 4 biswa given with water poured, as the translation reads, for Rayakuka.
items.gloss: Rayakuka ... with water poured (in the hand) donated 4 biswa.

items.note: Explains the royal 'five instruments' (shringa horn, tamata, conch, bheri, jayaghanta) as marks of the king's presence, played before officials granted this honour; background for the 'five-sound' title in the inscription.
items.gloss: The tradition of playing five instruments by the royal band showed the king's presence in the royal court. These five instruments included the shringa (horn), tamata (a drum), conch, bheri and jayaghanta. The tradition was to play them in front of the king, the royal family or any officials given this honour by the king's special favour.

reject_reason: scene from the Ramayana television serial; no bearing on Udaypur or any unit

items.note: Asks what a 4-biswa gift means after a temple built over two decades; Verma notes such small grants are not unique, with comparable records of the Chauhans of Naddula and Shakambhari and the Chalukyas of Gujarat; the plot cannot be identified today.
items.gloss: Now the question: after building a huge temple like Udaypur, whose construction took two decades, what could be the meaning of a king donating only a small piece of land like 4 biswa to the temple? Verma says this is not the only example of such seemingly minor land grants. In that period some records of the Chauhans of Naddula and Shakambhari in Rajasthan and the Chalukyas of Gujarat contain donations of small plots for religious purposes. From this inscription it is not possible today to identify that valuable piece of land in or around Udaypur.

claim.value: temple construction took two decades (this author)

items.note: Author's conjecture on why 4 biswa was notable: it may have had a water source for the temple's water supply, been a residence for the chief priest or manager, or held a fine stepwell whose water was reserved for the sanctum; not stated in the source inscription.
items.gloss: It is possible that this plot, small in size, had some special quality. It may have been full of water sources so that water supply for this temple could be ensured. It may have been given for the residential use of the royal priest or chief manager, or there may have been a splendid stepwell on it whose water was specially reserved for worship, abhisheka or rituals in the sanctum. If mention of so little land is inscribed on such a huge temple, its use too must have been of a very special kind.

items.note: Proposal made to the ASI Regional Director in March 2021: display Hindi-English translations of select inscriptions in the temple complex and post skilled staff at such sites.
items.gloss: In March 2021 we both met the ASI regional director Dr. P. K. Mishra at his office in Bhopal, and our suggestion was that in the huge temple complex of Udaypur Hindi-English translations of select inscriptions that give tourists new information should be displayed. Now people come. They have darshan. They stroll a little and leave without any information, into nothingness. Besides, the most skilled employees should be posted at such places, who themselves have an interest in raising the lustre of such places. They should not be like the unskilled workers of MNREGA.

items.note: Heading '42 monuments, 100 inscriptions'; INTACH credited with the most important role in bringing out Udaypur's story and detailed documentation.
items.gloss: 42 monuments, 100 inscriptions. The role of the Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage (INTACH) has been most important in bringing out Udaypur's story from outside Udaypur and in its detailed documentation, combing the desolate lanes of Udaypur.

items.note: INTACH Bhopal convener Dr. Madanmohan Upadhyay, a retired IAS officer, deployed an expert team that combed Udaypur for the first time.
items.gloss: As soon as our solitary efforts in Udaypur came to his notice, he deployed an expert team of INTACH in Udaypur. This team combed every inch of Udaypur for the first time.

items.note: The team identified remains from every ruler over a thousand to twelve hundred years, counted and documented the inscriptions; publication was about to follow after a year.
items.gloss: They had identified the remains from the time of every ruler who came and went over a long period of a thousand to twelve hundred years, counted the inscriptions and documented them. After a year the publication of this latest research centred on Udaypur is now also going to appear.

items.note: Upadhyay's assessment: Udaypur can become an example and an international tourist spot; he says he has not seen such diverse monuments anywhere in the world.
items.gloss: Dr. Upadhyay says that it can truly become an example. Udaypur has the capacity to be brought up as a splendid tourist spot on the international level. I have not seen so many diverse monuments together anywhere in the world.

items.note: Upadhyay: sites with a tenth of Udaypur's potential are crowded because of government policy; Udaypur can be a model; 'we are sitting on a treasure of history'.
items.gloss: Historical places with ten times less potential are more full of tourist bustle only because of governance policies. Udaypur can become a model in itself. Understand that in Udaypur we are sitting on a treasure of history.

items.note: The famous Nilakantheshwar temple is recorded in the Udaypur inscriptions as the Udayeshvara temple; no contemporary inscription names Nilakantheshwar and nobody knows when that name became famous.
items.gloss: The Nilakantheshwar temple, whose fame is far and wide, is recorded in the inscriptions of Udaypur as the Udayeshvara temple. Nowhere in contemporary inscriptions is the name Nilakantheshwar. In which century it became famous, nobody knows.

items.note: Nearly a hundred inscriptions survive, in Sanskrit, Persian and Devanagari, some with Sanskrit and Persian text together.
items.gloss: Most important of all, nearly a hundred inscriptions are available which have survived despite the buffeting of centuries of history. These are in Devanagari besides Sanskrit and Persian. There are also inscriptions in which Sanskrit and Persian texts occur together.

items.note: Udaypur said to hold old havelis, palaces, old bazaars, fort walls, temples, ancient tanks and stepwells: every remnant of a developed town plan.
items.gloss: This is the only place where there are old havelis, palaces, old markets, fort walls, temples, ancient tanks and stepwells. Every remnant of a developed town layout is present here.

items.note: INTACH's groundwork identified 42 new monuments needing urgent care; five or six ancient stepwells survive in much better condition.
items.gloss: But the INTACH team in its groundwork has identified 42 new monuments whose care is very necessary and which are being ruined with time. Five or six ancient stepwells have survived in much better condition till now.

items.note: Jain images on hill rocks, as at Gwalior and Chanderi, show the region held all religious traditions.
items.gloss: The availability of Jain images on hill rocks like Gwalior and Chanderi shows that this whole area had held within itself all kinds of religious traditions.

items.note: Mosques of the Muslim period after the Delhi sultans and emperors add new pages to Udaypur's story.
items.gloss: After coming under the sway of the sultans and emperors of Delhi, mosques of the Muslim period add some new pages to Udaypur's story.

items.note: Author's reading of Dr. Upadhyay's statement: every broken image at Udaypur, Hindu or Tirthankara, shows Udaypur too heard the hooves of Islamic invaders' horses (author's interpretation).
items.gloss: On Dr. Upadhyay's statement, my belief is that every broken image of Udaypur, whether of Hindu deities or Tirthankaras, shows that Udaypur too had heard the hoofbeats of the horses of the dull-minded followers of Islam.

items.note: INTACH's proposed plan to bring together ASI, state archaeology, district administration, panchayat, private bodies, corporates and the aware local society.
items.gloss: Based on this intensive groundwork, INTACH's future plan is that to raise Udaypur, the Archaeological Survey of India, state archaeology department, district administration, panchayat, private organisations, corporate companies and the aware local society should be brought together.

items.note: Upadhyay says locals have been distant and indifferent to their heritage; without their involvement outside or government efforts will not yield results.
items.gloss: Upadhyay visited Udaypur many times in the last year. He believes that local people have a separate world and their living connection with their priceless heritage has not been such that they take any effective initiative on their own. There has been a distance full of a kind of indifference. Until they feel attached to it, expected results cannot come from outside efforts or government efforts alone.

items.note: Government could make towns like Udaypur shine in PPP mode like historical places in Rajasthan and south India.
items.gloss: The government can make towns like Udaypur shine in PPP mode like the historical places of Rajasthan and South India. There is so much here to see and understand.

items.note: Proposal: state government should have panchayats comprehensively documented, as INTACH is doing in 10-12 districts.
items.gloss: Based on the Udaypur experience he says that if the state government gets panchayats comprehensively documented it will be a big initiative. We are doing this work in 10-12 districts. If the government does this work in all the panchayats of the state, it is certain that many priceless things will come to our notice together for the first time. We shall learn what is of archaeological importance in panchayats and villages.

items.note: Documentation is said to be a one-week job if local voluntary organisations are motivated and given a little training.
items.gloss: It is a job that can be done in a week. Only local voluntary organisations need to be motivated for this work. With a little training they will be able to list everything.

items.note: Before going to Udaypur they did not know inscriptions existed there in such large numbers everywhere; the temple alone could support a PhD on its inscriptions.
items.gloss: Before going to Udaypur we did not know that such a large number of inscriptions were present everywhere. On the inscriptions in the temple alone a complete PhD could be done.

items.note: Upadhyay notes a famine of epigraph readers in Madhya Pradesh, even in government departments and institutions.
items.gloss: Upadhyay points out that there is a famine of experts who can read inscriptions in Madhya Pradesh. Even in government departments and educational institutions there are no people who can read new inscriptions. For them it is as good as black letters. They will not be able to tell what is written on which stone.

items.note: Upadhyay: 30-plus princely houses of present-day Madhya Pradesh, much heritage in ruins; untouched chapters need a social campaign that cannot succeed without active local participation.
items.gloss: In present-day Madhya Pradesh there must have been more than 30 kings and princely states contemporary with British rule. Most of their heritage is turning into ruins. Its upkeep is not proper. The successors of the kings have moved to other places. In many places they do not survive. In such a case, to know the untouched chapters of history in detail a social campaign is needed, and its fruit is not possible without the active participation of the local society.

items.note: Nearby villages: Muradpur, where a huge Varaha image may once have stood in an ancient temple, and Sonari on a local river, known for sculptures coming out of its ground.
items.gloss: Such as Muradpur, where a huge image of Varaha must once have been in an ancient temple. Now it is a desolate place. Even nearer is Sonari village, settled on the bank of a local river, which is also famous for the sculptures that come out of its womb.

items.note: At Sonari, 5 km from Baretha station, the river yields broken and whole sculptures, mostly Vishnu avatars, including a Varaha masterpiece; some are in Vidisha museum.
items.gloss: When the water dries up the river spews out broken and whole sculptures. Sculptures found here are kept safe in village houses. Govind says most of the images are of the avatars of Lord Vishnu. Many images are kept on a veranda and some are in the premises of the District Archaeological Museum Vidisha. Among them is a masterpiece of Varaha avatar, which by luck survived whole. It was in a pair, the other part of which went to the museum.

items.note: A Vishnu image was recovered from smugglers about 15 years earlier; the area is fertile ground for idol thieves; villagers resist taking images out of the village.
items.gloss: A Vishnu image named Vishwa Mohan was recovered from smugglers about 15 years ago. It too is in Vidisha museum. This area has been extremely fertile for idol smugglers. Village people oppose taking these often-found images out of the village. They say they should be conserved here so that people coming from outside also take notice of Sonari village.

items.note: Author infers from Vishnu images found from Muradpur to Sonari a link to Gupta rulers, Vishnu worshippers, and building activity five hundred years before Udayaditya (author's inference).
items.gloss: The finding of Vishnu images from Muradpur to Sonari connects the threads of history to the Gupta rulers, who were worshippers of Vishnu, even further back than the Paramaras. From this we can guess that even five hundred years before Udayaditya the process of creating wonders of architecture was continuous here.

items.note: Author's interpretation: after the Turk conquest of Delhi in the late 12th century, temples were broken and broken images thrown into rivers; Sonari's broken images are taken as proof (author's view).
items.gloss: It is no longer hidden from anyone that after the Turk Muslim occupation of Delhi at the end of the 12th century, in the following centuries the ancient heritage all over the country came under threat. Wherever they went they proved destructive for temples and images. The tradition of building ghats, temples and gurukuls on river banks was not new. Temples were broken and the broken images thrown into rivers. The broken images of Sonari village are proof of that same belief of centuries ago, about which nothing was ever taught in our schools and colleges. They are evidence of the destructive power of Islam, which has by birth considered idol worship a sin.

items.note: Patari, about 15 km from Udaypur and midway between them on Google Maps, has ruins suggesting a developed town in Mauryan and Gupta times.
items.gloss: Once I went to a place about 15 km from Udaypur towards Patari, in picturesque green hills. If you join Udaypur and Patari on Google Maps, this place lies right in the middle. The ruins of Patari clearly show that it must have been a developed town in the time of the Mauryas and Gupta kings.

items.note: Hill forest with dense monsoon grass and teak forest, in Ganj Basoda tehsil of Vidisha district, with a small old fort called a gadhi.
items.gloss: But the place I went to is still not easy to reach directly by any vehicle. It is a hill forest. On this hill, surrounded by dense tall grass grown by the rain and thick teak forest, there is some old small fort that cannot be seen even from ten feet away. In nearby villages it is called a gadhi. It too is in Ganj Basoda tehsil of Vidisha district.

items.note: Notes that documents seldom answer who built such a gadhi, but local lore abounds: stories heard from elders and passed down.
items.gloss: ... but in folk tradition, around any such place, there are always many stories. Here too there are. Stories heard from elders in the family. Tales heard for generations. From these tales you can weave the fabric of an original story.

items.note: A recent Hanuman temple at Gayasi's gadhi holds a few centuries-old images broken in a way that suggests deliberate breakage.
items.gloss: The temple in rustic style is only about forty years old, but a few images give centuries-old testimony. They are broken in such a way as to show they were deliberately broken.

items.note: Village groups gather to recite Sundarkand; an unshakable belief that remembering 'Gadhi wale Babba' averts trouble.
items.gloss: A local officer gave the shape of a temple here by installing it. Now groups from villages gather here to recite Sundarkand. If any crisis comes, just remember Gadhi wale Babba and nothing will happen. There is such unshakable belief.

items.note: Deserted villages such as Daulatpur survive only as names; markets once met here.
items.gloss: Another thread: a village named Daulatpur was below, which is now deserted. There were more villages like it of which no trace remains. Only names. No villages. Markets once met here. But how did the villages become deserted?

items.note: Author's explanation: under Muslim rule raids and plunder were intense and Hindus camped in safe hills.
items.gloss: Third thread: in the rule of Muslims, attacks and plunder were intense. Hindus used to camp in such safe hills to save their lives and honour. This was such a safe place.

items.note: Bagdi described as a branch of local Rajputs who rebelled against Muslim rulers; descendants in the area now registered as Scheduled Caste, in the general category in Raisen district (author's account).
items.gloss: Fourth thread: the Bagdis were a branch of local Rajputs who rebelled or revolted and did not obey the orders of Muslim rulers. They lived here in an organised way. Their descendants are in the area even today, but after independence they got their names registered in the Scheduled Caste for the benefit of reservation. In Raisen district the branches of these same Bagdis are in the general category. Basically these are remnants of the era of slavery to Muslim rule.

items.note: Local lore of treasure hunters digging at the gadhi, most going mad, a few said to have found wealth.
items.gloss: Fifth thread: greedy people from far and wide came to the gadhi in search of treasure. They dug a lot. Most went mad. In the surrounding area there are stories of many beliefs that concerned the gadhi. Fortune also favoured some. There are tales of those who found wealth here.
